title: Psychology in One Level
objective: After this level you can explain what psychology studies, how psychologists test their ideas and what its main areas are.
summary: Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behavior. Since no one can read minds, psychologists measure what they can observe, and the field spans many areas.

cards.headline: Does a bird sing because it's happy? Science can't say.
cards.body: Nobody can measure a bird's happiness, so the idea can't be tested. Yet psychology, the scientific study of the mind and behavior, faces a version of that problem every day. How do you study something you can't see? And why does the field reach from memory to friendship?

cards.headline: From soul-study to science
cards.body: The word psychology joins Greek psykhe, "breath, spirit, soul", with -logia, "study of". So the name promises a study of the soul. The modern job description is more down to earth: psychology is the scientific study of the mind and behavior. The soul part got quietly retired; the curiosity stayed.

mascot.line: Keep this one: psychology measures what it can observe and reasons its way to the mind behind it.

cards.headline: Measuring what you can't see
cards.body: Nobody can read another person's mind, so psychologists work indirectly. They measure what they can observe: behavior, biological signals and self-reports, meaning what people tell them. From those, they infer what the mind is doing. That rescues half the bird puzzle: you can't quiz a bird, but you can ask people whether they sing because they're happy. Then psychologists publish their results so others can repeat the test and check.

cards.headline: Say "psychologist" and most people picture a couch.
cards.body: Clinical psychology gets the most attention in films and news, so many people assume all psychology is clinical. It isn't. And the person beside the couch might not be a psychologist at all. Who does what?

cards.headline: Most psychologists never sit by a couch
cards.body: Clinical psychologists diagnose and treat psychological disorders, and counseling psychologists help people who are generally healthy with emotional, social and career goals. But forensic psychologists work in the justice system, judging whether someone is competent to stand trial or advising on eyewitness testimony. Industrial-organizational psychologists work on workplaces, school psychologists work in education, and many psychologists teach and run research at universities. Prescribing, though, stays with medical training: that is why the psychiatrist can do it.

cards.fact: "Therapist" is a broad title. "Licensed psychologist" takes an exam.
cards.context: In the United States, only people who meet state requirements and pass a licensure exam can call themselves licensed clinical or counseling psychologists. So a psychologist's title is earned twice: once with a doctorate, once with a license.

title: The First Psychology Lab
objective: After this level you can explain what Wilhelm Wundt measured in his 1879 Leipzig lab and why it marks psychology's start as a science.
summary: In 1879 Wilhelm Wundt opened the first psychology lab in Leipzig. He timed reactions to a thousandth of a second and trained people to report their own experience.

cards.headline: Psychology's first lab could time you to a thousandth of a second.
cards.body: For centuries, the mind was something to argue about. Then, in 1879, a German scientist named Wilhelm Wundt started measuring it. What was he timing, and why does that date mark the start of psychology as a science?

cards.headline: Leipzig, 1879
cards.body: Wundt had a medical degree and taught physiology, the science of how the body works. In 1879 he set up the first psychology laboratory, at the University of Leipzig in Germany. Until then, psychology had been treated as a branch of philosophy, settled by argument. Wundt insisted on experiments, borrowing his methods from the natural sciences. The mind moved from the armchair to the lab bench.

cards.headline: Press the button when you see the light
cards.body: A typical Wundt experiment was simple. A participant, sometimes in a separate room, received a light, an image or a sound, then pressed a button. An apparatus recorded the reaction time to one-thousandth of a second. It sounds humble, but it was a breakthrough: a mental event, noticing and responding, turned into a number anyone could check.
cards.callout: Reaction time: how long it takes to respond to a signal

cards.headline: Looking inward, with training
cards.body: Wundt also used introspection. Trained observers examined their own conscious experience as objectively as they could, trying to break it into basic parts. The trouble was that introspection stayed highly subjective. Even after training, there was very little agreement between people. When two careful observers look inside and report different things, who settles it?

title: Freud and the Unconscious
objective: After this level you can explain Freud's idea of an unconscious mind and which parts of his theory failed when tested.
summary: Freud pictured most of the mind as hidden and unconscious. His specific theories mostly failed later tests, but the broad idea of unconscious mental life has research support.

cards.headline: Freud said you see only the tip of your own mind.
cards.body: He compared the mind to an iceberg: only about one-tenth of it conscious, the rest hidden below the waterline. It's one of the most famous pictures in psychology. How much of it survived testing?

cards.headline: The doctor who listened
cards.body: Sigmund Freud was an Austrian neurologist, a medical doctor rather than a psychologist. He saw the unconscious mind as a store of feelings and urges we aren't aware of. To reach it, he looked at dreams, at the first words that come to mind, and at slips of the tongue. His talking treatment, psychoanalysis, is still used today. Where Wundt's observers studied what they could notice, Freud went looking for what they couldn't.

cards.headline: Where the theory cracked
cards.body: Freud's evidence was mostly himself: his own recollections and his interpretations of his patients' stories and dreams. He treated that as enough proof that his stages of childhood development applied to everyone. When researchers later tested ideas like these, most of his specific claims found no support. An interpretation can feel convincing and still be wrong; that's exactly why science checks.

mascot.line: Keep the split: the broad idea of an unconscious survived testing, while most of Freud's specific claims did not.

cards.headline: What survived
cards.body: Freud wasn't simply wrong, either. In 1998, the psychologist Drew Westen reviewed the evidence and found a large body of research supporting two of Freud's broad ideas: much of mental life happens outside awareness, and childhood experience helps shape personality. The big picture held; most of the details sank.

title: Behaviorism: Only What You Can See
objective: After this level you can explain why behaviorists like John Watson and B. F. Skinner studied only observable behavior.
summary: In 1913 John Watson argued psychology should study only observable behavior. B. F. Skinner studied how consequences shape it, and behaviorism dominated for decades.

cards.headline: In 1913, a psychologist proposed leaving the mind out of psychology.
cards.body: John B. Watson argued that psychology should be a purely objective science of behavior, with no need for introspection. Why would a science of the mind drop the mind?

cards.headline: Watson's manifesto
cards.body: Watson's 1913 paper declared that psychology, as the behaviorist sees it, is a purely objective, experimental branch of natural science. Its goal: to predict and control behavior. Introspection, he wrote, forms no essential part of its methods. Remember how Wundt's trained observers kept disagreeing? Watson believed the mind couldn't be analyzed objectively at all, so he studied what anyone could watch: behavior.

cards.headline: Skinner: it's all in the consequences
cards.body: B. F. Skinner, another behaviorist, focused on how behavior is changed by its consequences. Reinforcement and punishment, in his view, were major forces driving what we do. Behaviorists often experimented on animals, like rats in the chamber that became known as the Skinner box, assuming the results would apply, to some degree, to people too. Chapter 3 opens that box properly.

cards.fact: Behaviorism ruled experimental psychology for decades.
cards.context: Especially in North America, it dominated through the 1950s. Its insistence on objective methods, above all experiments, helped establish psychology as a science. And its ideas never left: they still shape behavioral therapy and classroom techniques today.

title: The Cognitive Revolution
objective: After this level you can explain how psychologists in the 1950s and 1960s began studying the mind as a processor of information.
summary: From the 1950s, computers, linguistics and neuroscience brought the mind back. Chomsky showed behaviorism couldn't explain language, and psychology modeled the mind as an information processor.

cards.headline: A new machine gave psychologists a new picture of the mind.
cards.body: Around 1956, computers had existed for only a few years. They stored information, followed step-by-step procedures and produced answers. Could a mind work something like that? The question pulled psychology out of the behaviorist era.

cards.headline: The mind comes back
cards.body: Behaviorism dominated North American psychology through the 1950s. But by then, new work in linguistics, neuroscience and computer science was reviving interest in the mind as something science could study. This shift became known as the cognitive revolution. Psychologists wanted to know again what happens between the signal going in and the behavior coming out.

cards.headline: Chomsky's challenge
cards.body: In 1959 the linguist Noam Chomsky reviewed B. F. Skinner's book on verbal behavior and argued that behaviorism couldn't explain how young children learn language so fast. By age four or five, children understand and produce sentences they have never heard. Chomsky argued that language learning doesn't depend on detailed reinforcement. Nobody rewarded you for your first brand-new sentence; you just built it.

cards.headline: The mind as an information processor
cards.body: Most cognitive science since then assumes the mind holds representations, a bit like a computer's stored data, and runs procedures on them, a bit like a program's steps. In 1967 Ulric Neisser published the first textbook titled Cognitive Psychology, giving the new field its name on a cover.

title: Nature, Nurture or Both?
objective: After this level you can explain how twin and adoption studies separate the effects of genes and upbringing.
summary: Twin studies compare identical and fraternal twins, and adoption studies compare biological and adoptive relatives. Across 50 years of twin studies, heritability averaged 49 percent.

cards.headline: Psychologists can't swap babies between families. Families do it for them.
cards.body: Ethics rule out many experiments psychologists might like to run, like assigning children to different homes. But twins and adopted children already provide the comparison. How do they help untangle genes from upbringing?

cards.headline: Twins and adoptees
cards.body: Identical twins have almost no differences in their DNA, while fraternal twins share on average 50 percent of theirs. So twin studies compare how often a trait is shared by identical versus fraternal twins. If identical twins raised together are more alike on a trait than fraternal twins, genes likely play a role. Adoption studies flip the setup: they compare children with their biological relatives and with the family that raised them.

cards.fact: Across 50 years of twin studies, the average heritability was 49 percent.
cards.context: In 2015, Tinca Polderman and colleagues pooled virtually every twin study published over 50 years: 17,804 traits and about 14.5 million twin pairs. Averaged across all traits, heritability came out at 49 percent. Roughly half of the differences between people traced to genetic differences, and the rest to everything else.

mascot.line: People mix up "heritable" and "fixed" all the time. Highly heritable hair color still changes with dye.

cards.headline: What heritability does not mean
cards.body: Heritability describes differences within a population, not a person. A heritability of 0.7 doesn't mean a trait is 70 percent caused by genes; it means 70 percent of the variation between people in that group comes from genetic differences, in that environment. It also isn't destiny. The language you speak runs in families yet has a heritability of zero. Hair color is highly heritable, and one bottle of dye changes it.

title: How Psychologists Study People
objective: After this level you can tell apart case studies, surveys, observation and experiments, and what each can and can't show about the mind.
summary: Case studies go deep on a few people, observation watches behavior unnoticed, and surveys reach many people but rely on honest answers. Only experiments show cause.

cards.headline: Ask a class who always washes their hands after the restroom.
cards.body: Almost every hand may go up, because many people aren't comfortable answering that honestly. So how do you find out what people really do? Psychologists have several tools, and each one has a blind spot.

cards.headline: Case study: deep but narrow
cards.body: A case study focuses on one person or just a few, and no other single method gathers such rich detail. The catch is the reason people get studied this way: they often have something rare about them. That makes findings hard to generalize to everyone else. Remember Freud building theories from his own patients' stories in Level 4? Deep knowledge of a few people can't tell you about everyone.

cards.headline: Watching without being noticed
cards.body: Naturalistic observation means watching behavior in its natural setting, and observers try hard to go unnoticed. People who know they're watched behave less naturally; think of how you'd drive with a police car behind you. In 1960 Jane Goodall began observing wild chimpanzees at Gombe, in Tanzania, a famous example. The prize is realism. The price is control: you can't make the behavior happen on schedule.

cards.headline: Surveys: many people, thinner answers
cards.body: Surveys are lists of questions, and they make it easy to collect answers from large numbers of people. They pay for that with depth, and with a bigger weakness: self-reports. People lie, misremember, or answer to look good, like reporting drinking less alcohol than they do. Hello again, hand washers. None of these methods can prove what causes what; only an experiment can.

title: Rules That Protect Participants
objective: After this level you can explain informed consent and ethics review boards, and the studies that made them necessary.
summary: Abuses like Nazi experiments and the Tuskegee syphilis study led to consent rules and ethics review boards. Today participants must know the risks and can quit anytime.

cards.headline: Before a study on people starts, a committee has to say yes.
cards.body: In the United States, a review board generally has to approve research on people before it begins. That wasn't always so. The rules exist because of studies that did serious harm to people who never agreed to it.

events.label: The US Public Health Service starts a syphilis study in Alabama without consent

cards.headline: The Tuskegee study
cards.body: In 1932 the US Public Health Service began studying syphilis in 600 Black men in Alabama, 399 with the disease and 201 without. Their informed consent was never collected. The men with syphilis were not told they had it, and when penicillin became an effective treatment in the 1940s, they were not given it. The study ran until 1972, when the press exposed it. The outrage led directly to the National Research Act of 1974.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing: consent means knowing the risks, choosing freely and being free to stop.

cards.headline: What protection looks like today
cards.body: Now an institutional review board, a committee of scientists, administrators and community members, reviews a study before it can proceed. Participants give informed consent: they learn what to expect, including risks, and know they can quit at any time without penalty, with their data kept confidential. Parents sign for anyone under 18. If a study used deception, everyone gets a full, honest debriefing at the end. It's also why some questions, like swapping babies between families, stay off-limits.

cards.headline: From armchair to laboratory
cards.body: Attempts to understand the mind go back at least to Greek philosophers such as Plato and Aristotle. From then on, the study of mind stayed part of philosophy until the nineteenth century, when experimental psychology developed. By the late 1800s psychology was accepted as its own academic discipline, and Wilhelm Wundt in Germany and William James in the United States are generally credited as its founders.

title: Sensing Versus Perceiving
objective: After this level you can tell sensation from perception and explain how the mind turns raw signals into experience.
summary: Sensation is your receptors detecting a stimulus and turning it into nerve signals. Perception is organizing and interpreting those signals into experience, and the two can come apart.

cards.headline: A light can flash in your window all night, and you stop seeing it.
cards.body: Your eyes still register every flash. You just stop noticing it. That gap, between what your senses pick up and what you actually experience, is where the psychology of perception begins. So what exactly is the difference?

cards.headline: Step one: sensation
cards.body: Sensation happens when a sensory receptor, a specialized nerve cell, detects something. Light entering your eye causes changes in cells at the back of it, and those cells relay messages to your brain and spinal cord. Converting light, sound or pressure into nerve signals is called transduction. The Human Body tree covers the hardware. The point here: at this stage nothing has been understood yet. It's raw data.

cards.headline: Step two: perception
cards.body: Perception is the way that sensory information is organized, interpreted and consciously experienced. One textbook puts it neatly: sensation is a physical process, perception a psychological one. Walk into a kitchen where cinnamon rolls are baking. The sensation is your scent receptors detecting cinnamon. The perception might be "this smells like Grandma's holiday baking." Same molecules, very different experience.

cards.headline: Sensed, but not perceived
cards.body: Perceptions are built from sensations, but not every sensation becomes a perception. When a stimulus stays constant for a long time, you often stop perceiving it even though your receptors still sense it. That's sensory adaptation, and it's why you don't feel the weight of your clothes or hear the hum of a projector. Back to the flashing light: sensed every time, perceived less and less. Two different jobs.

title: The Smallest Change You Notice
objective: After this level you can explain the just-noticeable difference and Weber's law.
summary: The just-noticeable difference is the smallest change you detect half the time. Weber's law (1834) says it is a constant fraction of what you start with, so bigger stimuli need bigger changes.

cards.headline: A phone lights up in a dark cinema. Everyone notices.
cards.body: In a brightly lit basketball arena, the same screen goes almost unseen. Its brightness is identical. What changed is what it's competing with, and psychologists have had a law for that since 1834.

cards.headline: The just-noticeable difference
cards.body: How much must something change before you notice? That amount is the just-noticeable difference, also called the difference threshold: the smallest difference between two stimuli needed to tell them apart. Your sensitivity drifts through the day and with whatever you've just experienced, so psychologists define it as the smallest difference you detect 50 percent of the time.

mascot.line: Keep this one: noticing a change depends on the fraction, not the amount.

cards.headline: Weber's weights
cards.body: In 1834 the German physiologist Ernst Heinrich Weber described the rule, from research on lifting weights. Try it with a friend. Hand them a 1-pound object, then a 2-pound one: they'll tell the difference every time. Now try 10 pounds, then 11. Much harder, even though both pairs differ by exactly 1 pound.

cards.fact: The just-noticeable difference is a constant fraction of what you start with.
cards.context: That's Weber's law: bigger stimuli need bigger changes to be noticed. One pound is a big fraction of 1 pound and a small fraction of 10. It also explains the phone: many people notice it in a dark cinema, very few in a bright arena. The law isn't perfect; it has been shown not to hold at the extremes of stimulation.

title: Seeing Wholes, Not Parts
objective: After this level you can explain the Gestalt grouping principles and how they organize what you see.
summary: From Wertheimer's 1912 study of apparent motion, Gestalt psychologists argued the whole differs from the sum of its parts, and described how we group what we see.

cards.headline: Motion that isn't there

Its motto: the whole is different from the sum of its parts.

title: You See What You Expect
objective: After this level you can explain how expectations and context shape perception, called top-down processing.
summary: Perception runs bottom-up from the stimulus and top-down from knowledge and expectations. Expectations make reading fast, and make you skip a repeated word.

cards.headline: Read this out loud: Paris in the the spring.
cards.body: Did you catch the second "the"? Many readers skip right over it. The word was on the page. Your mind just didn't expect it.

cards.headline: Two directions of processing
cards.body: Psychologists describe two routes. In bottom-up processing, the stimulus drives perception: in a noisy restaurant, a crash of dropped plates grabs your attention whether you like it or not. In top-down processing, knowledge and expectations drive it. Hunting for keys on a yellow fob, you scan the counter and the coffee table for yellow, not the ceiling fan. Perception uses both routes.

cards.headline: Why you skipped the "the"
cards.body: The repeated word is top-down processing at work. You know the phrase, and a second "the" makes no sense, so your brain doesn't expect it and tends to skip it. A beginning reader, working carefully through each word from the bottom up, is less likely to make the mistake. Experience makes you a fast reader, and occasionally a sloppy one.

cards.headline: Hearing a phone that isn't ringing
cards.body: Waiting for an important call, you may think you hear the phone ringing in the shower when it isn't. Wanting to detect something shifts what you detect. Psychologists say perceptions rest on perceptual hypotheses, educated guesses shaped by your personality, experience and expectations, which together form your perceptual set. Because perception is built from sensations but shaped by experience and culture, two people can perceive the same scene very differently.

title: Hearing With Your Eyes
objective: After this level you can explain the McGurk effect and how the mind merges what you see with what you hear.
summary: In the McGurk effect, the sound "ba" with a face saying "ga" is often heard as "da": the brain merges sight and sound. How strongly people are fooled varies widely.

cards.headline: Your eyes can change what you hear.
cards.body: Play a recording of someone saying one syllable, but show a face mouthing a different one. Many people hear a third syllable that neither the voice nor the lips produced. Heard alone, without the video, the same sound is identified almost perfectly.

cards.headline: Hearing lips and seeing voices
cards.body: That's the McGurk effect, reported by Harry McGurk and John MacDonald in 1976 in a paper titled "Hearing lips and seeing voices". In their report, 98 percent of adults heard "da" when the sound "ba" was paired with a video of lips saying "ga". The mismatch doesn't make you hear the voice or read the lips: you hear a third syllable, different from both.

cards.headline: Why the brain blends
cards.body: Your brain integrates information from different senses, and it typically responds more strongly to sight and sound together than to the sum of each alone. That's useful: at a loud concert, watching a friend's lips helps you follow what they say, while in a quiet cafe you'd hardly need it. The McGurk effect is reported to be strongest when the sound is poor, when your eyes have the most to add.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the 98 percent. Remember the lesson: one famous number rarely tells the whole story.

cards.fact: In a 2015 study of 165 adults, some never heard the illusion and some heard it every time.

title: The Cocktail Party Effect

summary: Selective attention follows one voice and tunes out the rest, yet about a third of people catch their own name in a message they are ignoring.

cards.body: You weren't listening to them. So how did your name get through the noise?

cards.headline: One voice at a time
cards.body: Selective attention is the ability to pick out certain things to process while ignoring distractions. In a 1953 paper, Colin Cherry coined the term "cocktail-party problem" and took it into the lab: listeners heard a different message in each ear and repeated one aloud as they heard it, a task called shadowing. They could say little about what the ignored ear heard. Many didn't notice when it switched from English to German.

cards.headline: Your name breaks through
cards.body: If the ignored ear were truly shut off, your name couldn't get through either. Yet in Moray's 1959 study and a 1995 repeat by Wood and Cowan, about 33 percent of people reported hearing their own name in the message they were ignoring. Anne Treisman proposed an explanation: ignored information is turned down, not blocked, so something as meaningful as your name can still slip past.

cards.fact: In a 2021 replication, 29 percent noticed their own name. Unexpected words rarely got through.
cards.context: The study was preregistered, and the name effect held. And the people who caught their name tended to score lower on working-memory tests, which researchers read as more trouble blocking out distracting information.

title: The Invisible Gorilla
objective: After this level you can explain inattentional blindness and the basketball study that made it famous.
summary: While counting basketball passes, nearly half of viewers missed a person in a gorilla suit. Inattentional blindness catches experts too: most radiologists missed a gorilla in a lung scan.

cards.headline: Count the passes. You might miss the gorilla.
cards.body: In Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris's 1999 study, viewers watched people pass basketballs and counted the passes made by the team in white. Partway through, a person in a gorilla costume walked right through the game.

cards.headline: Nearly half missed it
cards.body: Nearly half of the people who watched didn't notice the gorilla at all, though it was clearly visible. Their attention was locked on counting, so everything else got tuned out. The name for this is inattentional blindness: failing to notice something completely visible because you're attending to something else.

cards.headline: What made it easier to miss
cards.body: The study also mapped when people miss things. Noticing depended on how similar the unexpected object was to the other things on screen, and on how hard the counting task was. It did not depend on how close the gorilla came to the action being watched. You attend to objects and events, not to patches of screen.

mascot.line: Keep this one: your eyes can land on something your attention never picks up.

cards.headline: Experts aren't immune
cards.body: In 2013, researchers asked 24 radiologists to search lung scans for nodules, a task they're trained for. In the last scan they inserted a gorilla 48 times the size of an average nodule. 83 percent of the radiologists didn't see it. Eye tracking showed that most of those who missed it had looked directly at its location.

title: The Multitasking Myth
objective: After this level you can explain why switching between tasks costs time and accuracy.
summary: Multitasking is mostly rapid switching, and each switch makes you slower and more error-prone. Phone conversations, even hands-free, pull attention from the road.

cards.headline: Doing two things at once? You're probably switching.
cards.body: Some researchers suggest that unless a task is fully automatic, multitasking is really your attention flicking back and forth between tasks. Switching sounds free. It isn't.

cards.headline: The switch cost
cards.body: In task-switching experiments, people alternate between simple tasks. Right after each switch, they respond substantially slower and usually make more errors. Psychologists call this the switch cost. A moment to prepare shrinks it, but doesn't make it disappear. In a 2001 study by Rubinstein and colleagues, the time lost grew as the rules of the tasks got more complex.

cards.headline: It's the conversation, not your hands
cards.body: In a 2001 driving-simulator study, phone conversations doubled the rate of missed traffic signals and slowed reactions to the ones drivers caught. Hands-free phones were no better than handheld ones. Listening to the radio or a book on tape didn't hurt at all. Later eye-tracking studies found that drivers on the phone were less likely to recognize things they had looked at, a form of inattentional blindness.

cards.fact: In a 2010 study of 200 people, 2.5 percent, about 1 in 40, showed no cost at all.
cards.context: Researchers called them supertaskers: they drove in a simulator while doing a demanding memory and math task with no drop in performance. For everyone else, combining the tasks made performance worse.

title: The Subliminal Popcorn Hoax
objective: After this level you can explain what subliminal perception can and cannot do, and why the 1957 movie theater claim was made up.
summary: In 1957 James Vicary claimed hidden "Eat Popcorn" messages boosted cinema sales; he later admitted he made it up. Subliminal effects are real in the lab but small, and depend on what you already want.

cards.headline: In 1957, hidden words on a movie screen supposedly sold popcorn.
cards.body: Market researcher James Vicary claimed that briefly flashing "Eat Popcorn" during a movie, below conscious awareness, raised popcorn sales by more than 50 percent. If true, advertisers could steer you without your knowing. Was it true?

cards.headline: Below the threshold
cards.body: To be detected, a stimulus has to be strong enough. The absolute threshold is the minimum amount of stimulus energy you detect 50 percent of the time. A message below the threshold for conscious awareness is subliminal: you receive it, but you aren't aware of it. Vicary's claim was that subliminal words could change what people bought.

cards.headline: It never happened
cards.body: Vicary later admitted the study was made up. Nobody has ever replicated his findings. One of the most famous claims for subliminal persuasion was a hoax.

cards.headline: What hidden messages can do
cards.body: Lab research shows people can process and respond to information outside awareness. But hidden messages have little effect on behavior outside the lab. In a 2006 study, subliminally flashing the drink brand Lipton Ice increased choice of that brand, but only among participants who were already thirsty. It nudged a choice people were ready to make; it didn't create the thirst.

title: Pavlov's Dogs
objective: After this level you can explain classical conditioning using Ivan Pavlov's experiments with dogs.
summary: Studying digestion, Ivan Pavlov noticed dogs drooling before food arrived. Pairing a tone with food, he showed how a neutral signal becomes a conditioned stimulus.

cards.headline: A Nobel Prize winner in digestion is famous for drooling dogs.
cards.body: Ivan Pavlov won the 1904 Nobel Prize for his work on how digestion works. Yet the experiment everyone remembers is about dogs drooling at a sound. What was a digestion expert doing in a psychology course?

cards.headline: The drool that came too early
cards.body: Pavlov was a physiologist, and his dogs were there to help him study digestion. He measured how much saliva they made in response to food. Then the dogs got ahead of him. They began to drool at the sight of food, at an empty bowl, even at the sound of the lab assistants' footsteps. Drooling at food in the mouth is a reflex; nobody has to learn it. Drooling at footsteps is different. Those dogs had learned something.

cards.headline: Sound first, then food
cards.body: So Pavlov tested it. Meat powder was his unconditioned stimulus: it triggers drooling, the unconditioned response, with no learning needed. Just before the food, he sounded a tone, a neutral stimulus that at first meant nothing to the dogs. After he paired them over and over, the tone alone made the dogs drool. The tone had become a conditioned stimulus, and the drool it caused, a conditioned response. His sounds included a metronome and a buzzer, not just the famous bell.

cards.fact: Classical conditioning: learning that one stimulus predicts another.
cards.context: In classical conditioning, animals and people learn to associate stimuli, and so to anticipate events. Pavlov's dogs learned that the tone meant dinner was coming. John Watson, the founder of behaviorism you met in Level 5, drew on Pavlov's work and believed the same principles could condition human emotions too.

title: Unlearning a Response
objective: After this level you can explain extinction and spontaneous recovery in classical conditioning.
summary: Sound the tone without food and the drool fades: extinction. After a rest it returns: spontaneous recovery. Extinction adds new learning instead of erasing the old.

cards.headline: Sound the tone with no food, and the drooling stops. For a while.
cards.body: Once Pavlov's dogs drooled at a tone, he sounded it without the food, and soon they stopped responding. So is a learned response gone for good once it stops? The dogs had a surprise in store.

cards.headline: Extinction: the signal stops meaning anything
cards.body: Pavlov kept sounding the tone, his conditioned stimulus, but no meat powder followed. The drooling grew weaker and weaker, until there was none at all. This fading is called extinction: the conditioned response weakens once the unconditioned stimulus stops following the conditioned stimulus. A signal that no longer predicts anything stops getting a reaction. The tone was just a noise again. Or so it seemed.

cards.headline: The comeback
cards.body: Then Pavlov let the dogs rest. After a couple of hours away from extinction training, he sounded the tone again, and the dogs drooled. The response that had vanished came back on its own. Pavlov called this spontaneous recovery: an extinguished conditioned response returning after a rest. So extinction hadn't wiped the slate clean. Something of the old lesson was still in there.

mascot.line: Keep this one: extinction teaches a second lesson on top of the first. The first lesson is still underneath.

cards.headline: Painted over, not scraped off
cards.body: Later research explains the comeback. Extinction doesn't destroy the original learning. It adds a new lesson on top, roughly "the tone means nothing now", and that new lesson depends heavily on context. That's why an old response tends to return when time passes, which is spontaneous recovery, or when the animal is back where it first learned, which is called renewal. The old lesson was painted over, not scraped off.

title: Little Albert and Learned Fear
objective: After this level you can explain how Watson conditioned fear in an infant and why the study is criticized today.
summary: In 1920 Watson and Rayner paired a loud bang with a white rat until an infant feared it, and the fear spread to furry things. The study has serious flaws.

cards.headline: In 1920, two psychologists set out to teach a baby to be afraid.
cards.body: John Watson believed emotions could be conditioned just like Pavlov's drool. With his graduate student Rosalie Rayner, at Johns Hopkins University, he tested it on an infant their paper called Albert B. Here's what they did, and why it's criticized today.

cards.headline: A rat and a loud bang
cards.body: At first, Albert wasn't afraid of a white rat, a rabbit, a dog, masks or cotton wool. One thing did frighten him: a loud sound, made by striking a hammer on a steel bar behind him. It made him cry. So each time Albert touched the rat, Watson struck the bar. After repeated pairings, the rat alone frightened him. In Level 21's terms, the bang was the unconditioned stimulus, and the rat became a conditioned stimulus for fear.

cards.headline: Fear spreads to lookalikes
cards.body: Days later, Albert was also afraid of other furry things: a rabbit, a fur coat, even a Santa Claus mask. None of them had been part of the pairings. This is stimulus generalization: giving the conditioned response to things similar to the conditioned stimulus. The more alike they are, the more likely the response. Bad news for anyone in a Santa suit.

cards.headline: Why it's criticized
cards.body: The whole study rested on a single infant, a thin base for claims about how people learn fear. Watson and Rayner planned to remove the fears, but Albert left the hospital on the last day of testing, so they never did. By today's standards the study would be considered unethical. Even who Albert was is disputed: one research team named a boy in 2009, and another argued in 2014 that a different boy fit the records better.

title: One Bad Meal
objective: After this level you can explain conditioned taste aversion and why it can be learned in a single try.
summary: Get sick after a food and its taste can turn your stomach: conditioned taste aversion. It can form in one try, across hours, and biology makes it easy to learn.

cards.headline: Pavlov paired tone and food over and over. One bad meal can do it at once.
cards.body: Maybe you know the feeling: you got sick after a certain dish, and now its taste turns your stomach. That lesson can take a single try. Why is this kind of learning so fast?

cards.headline: One try is enough
cards.body: This is conditioned taste aversion. Something you eat gets linked with the nausea or illness that follows, so the taste itself comes to make you feel sick. In Level 21's terms, the taste is the conditioned stimulus, and feeling sick at it is the conditioned response. It breaks a rule, though. Pavlov paired the tone and food over and over, but a taste aversion can form after a single pairing.

cards.headline: Hours apart, still linked
cards.body: It breaks a second rule too. Most conditioning needs only a brief gap between the two stimuli. A taste aversion can form even when several hours pass between eating and getting sick. Of everything you did that afternoon, the meal takes the blame.

cards.headline: Garcia's rats
cards.body: In 1966, John Garcia and Robert Koelling gave thirsty rats flavored water that came with lights and sounds. Then some rats were made ill, and others got foot shocks. The sick rats avoided the flavor but not the lights and sounds; the shocked rats avoided the lights and sounds but not the flavor. So some links are easier to learn than others. Taste aversion may be an adaptation that helps animals quickly learn to avoid harmful food.

title: The Skinner Box
objective: After this level you can explain operant conditioning: how consequences change how often a behavior happens.
summary: Thorndike's law of effect says what works gets repeated. Skinner built on it with rats and pigeons in the Skinner box, and shaped complex behaviors step by step.

cards.headline: Pavlov's method can make a dog drool. It can't teach anyone to ride a bike.
cards.body: Classical conditioning works on reflexes an animal already has. Brand-new behaviors need another kind of learning, one driven by what happens after you act. The story starts with a cat in a box.

cards.headline: Thorndike's cats
cards.body: Edward Thorndike placed a cat in a box with a lever. Pressing the lever opened a door, and the cat could escape and get food. From experiments like this came his law of effect: behaviors followed by satisfying consequences are more likely to be repeated, and behaviors followed by unpleasant ones are less likely. In short, what works sticks.

mascot.line: This is the box Level 5 promised to open. Classical: signal first. Operant: consequence after.

cards.headline: Inside the Skinner box
cards.body: B. F. Skinner built on the law of effect. He studied mostly rats and pigeons in an operant conditioning chamber, now called the Skinner box. A rat presses a lever, or a pigeon pecks a disk, and food comes out; a recorder counts every response. This is operant conditioning: learning to link a behavior with its consequence. Mind the order. In classical conditioning the stimulus comes just before the response; here the consequence comes soon after the behavior.

cards.headline: Shaping, one small step at a time
cards.body: A pigeon won't play ping pong by accident, so Skinner used shaping. Reward any response that resembles the target behavior, then only closer ones, until only the full behavior earns food. With shaping, he taught pigeons to turn in circles, walk in figure eights and even play ping pong. Animal trainers still commonly use it today.

title: Reinforcement Versus Punishment
objective: After this level you can tell positive and negative reinforcement and punishment apart in everyday examples.
summary: Positive adds and negative removes; reinforcement raises a behavior and punishment lowers it. The seatbelt beep is negative reinforcement, and time-out is negative punishment.

cards.headline: Your car's seatbelt beep is a lesson in negative reinforcement.
cards.body: The beeping stops the moment you buckle up. That isn't punishment, even though "negative" sounds like it should be. Two questions sort out all four terms for good.

cards.headline: Two questions to ask
cards.body: Skinner's terms use everyday words in a special way. First question: is something added or taken away? Positive means added, negative means removed; neither means good or bad. Second question: does the behavior go up or down? Reinforcement increases it, punishment decreases it. Both follow the law of effect from Level 25: satisfying consequences make a behavior more likely, unpleasant ones less likely.

Negative: remove something pleasant, like a favorite toy

mascot.line: When in doubt, ask one thing: did the behavior go up? Then it's reinforcement, whatever the sign.

The beep ends when you buckle, so you buckle more: that's reinforcement. Time-out is the one that trips people up. It removes a child from an enjoyable activity to make a behavior less likely, so it's negative punishment.

title: Why Slot Machines Hook People
objective: After this level you can explain reinforcement schedules and why unpredictable rewards keep a behavior going longest.
summary: Rewards can come every time or only sometimes, by count or by time. Unpredictable variable ratio rewards, used in gambling, are the hardest to extinguish.

cards.headline: A slot machine pays after an unpredictable number of pulls. That's the trap.
cards.body: You'd think unpredictable rewards would make people give up sooner. The research on reward timing says the opposite. It comes down to the timing of rewards, known as reinforcement schedules.

cards.headline: Every time, or only sometimes
cards.body: Reward a behavior every single time and you're using continuous reinforcement. Reward it only some of the time and it's partial, or intermittent, reinforcement. Partial schedules come in four kinds, sorted by two questions. Is the reward based on how many responses you make (ratio) or on how much time has passed (interval)? And is that number fixed or variable?

items.label: Ratio: counts your responses

items.label: Interval: counts the time

cards.headline: Why the slot machine wins
cards.body: Most gambling runs on a variable ratio schedule: the next pull might pay, or the one after that, or much later. Each win adds money right after a pull, which is positive reinforcement, delivered unpredictably. Of the four schedules, variable ratio gets the most responding and is the most resistant to extinction; fixed interval is the easiest to extinguish. More broadly, behavior rewarded only now and then lasts longer once rewards stop than behavior rewarded every time, an effect long seen as central to why people keep gambling without winning.

title: Learning by Watching
objective: After this level you can explain observational learning and what Albert Bandura's Bobo doll study showed.
summary: In 1961, preschoolers who watched an adult attack a Bobo doll copied the attack. Bandura showed we learn by watching, and that consequences shape doing more than learning.

cards.headline: Nobody rewarded these preschoolers for hitting a doll. They did it anyway.
cards.body: Skinner's rats had to act and get rewarded to learn. In 1961, Albert Bandura showed that children could pick up a behavior just by watching someone else do it, odd details and all.

cards.headline: The Bobo doll study
cards.body: Bandura, Dorothea Ross and Sheila Ross had 72 preschoolers from the Stanford University Nursery School, aged about three to five, watch an adult in a room with a 5-foot inflated Bobo doll. Some saw the adult attack it: striking it with a mallet, sitting on it and punching it, saying "Pow" and "Sock him". Others saw a quiet adult. Later, in a different room with toys that included a Bobo doll and no adult to copy, the children who had watched the attack reproduced it, far more than the others.

cards.headline: Learning by watching
cards.body: This is observational learning: watching others, called models, and then imitating them. Bandura argued that pure behaviorism couldn't explain learning that happens without any reinforcement, so his social learning theory took mental processes into account. He described four steps: attention (you notice the model), retention (you remember), reproduction (you can do it) and motivation (you want to).

mascot.line: Keep this: what happens to a model mostly changes whether you act on it, not whether you learned it.

cards.headline: Learning isn't the same as doing
cards.body: In a 1965 study, some children saw the model punished for the attack. They imitated it less than children who saw the model rewarded or facing no consequence. Seeing a model rewarded makes you more motivated to copy, which is called vicarious reinforcement. Then Bandura offered the children rewards to copy the model, and the differences between groups disappeared. Even the children who saw the punishment had learned the moves. They just hadn't shown them.

title: How Habits Form
objective: After this level you can explain how a cue, a routine and a reward build a habit, and how long habits really take to form.
summary: Repeat a behavior in the same setting, with a reward, and the setting's cues come to trigger it automatically. In one study, habits took a median of 66 days.

cards.headline: How long does a new habit take to stick? One study counted.
cards.body: You probably brush your teeth without deciding to. That's a habit doing the work. Psychologists have mapped how habits form, and one team timed the process in real people. The answer is neither quick nor tidy.

cards.headline: Cue, routine, reward
cards.body: Habits grow out of repetition in one setting. You pursue a goal by doing the same thing in the same context, again and again. With each repetition, the link in memory between the context's cues, like a coffee filter on the counter, and your response gets a little stronger. The reward that follows, like the coffee itself, strengthens the link further. Eventually the cue alone sets off the routine, automatically.

cards.headline: The law of effect, on autopilot
cards.body: This builds on Thorndike's principle from Level 25: rewarded responses get repeated. A habit is what you get when that repetition goes on long enough in one setting that the cues take over. You stop choosing; the coffee filter chooses for you.

cards.fact: In one study, new daily habits took a median of 66 days to become automatic.
cards.context: Phillippa Lally's team had 96 volunteers pick an eating, drinking or activity behavior and do it daily in the same context, like after breakfast, for 12 weeks. The spread was huge: from 18 days to an estimated 254. Good news for the imperfect: missing one opportunity didn't materially set habit formation back.

cards.headline: What counts as learning
cards.body: Psychologists define learning as a relatively permanent change in behavior or knowledge that results from experience. Most of this chapter was associative learning: making connections between things that happen together, like a tone and food, or a lever and a pellet. Classical and operant conditioning both need direct experience. Observational learning stretches the reach, because you can learn by watching others.

title: Three Stops for a Memory
objective: After this level you can explain sensory, short-term and long-term memory and how information moves between them.
summary: Atkinson and Shiffrin (1968) proposed three stages of memory: sensory, short-term and long-term. Rehearsal moves information from short-term into long-term memory.

cards.headline: Your senses catch far more than you will ever remember.
cards.body: Sights, sounds and tastes pour in all day, and you can't absorb even most of them. What was your teacher wearing last class? Probably gone. So how does the small slice you keep become a memory that lasts for years?

mascot.line: Keep the route in mind: senses, short-term, long-term. The rest of this chapter follows memories along it.

cards.headline: Three stops on one route
cards.body: In 1968, psychologists Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin proposed that information passes through three stages on its way to storage: sensory memory, short-term memory and long-term memory. Their model treats memory the way a computer handles information: data comes in, gets worked on, and some of it gets saved. It isn't the only model of memory, but it gave psychologists a route to follow.

cards.headline: Stop one: a blink-length buffer
cards.body: Sensory memory holds sights, sounds and tastes for up to a couple of seconds. Most of what hits your senses doesn't matter to you, so your mind discards it. As long as your teacher's outfit was ordinary, it probably never got past this stop. Only what you treat as worth keeping moves on to short-term memory.

cards.headline: Stop two: use it or lose it
cards.body: Short-term memory holds information for only about 15 to 30 seconds. Then it's either discarded or moved into long-term memory, and rehearsal does the moving. Repeating something works. Linking it to what you already know works too, like remembering a new friend's area code because your uncle's is the same. Long-term memory's capacity is believed to be unlimited. The bottleneck isn't space; it's getting through the door.

title: Holding Things in Mind
objective: After this level you can explain working memory's small capacity and how chunking stretches it.
summary: Working memory holds the few thoughts you are using right now. Miller put its limit at seven, plus or minus two; later research says about four chunks, and chunking packs more into each one.

cards.headline: Try holding 5205550467 in your head. Now try 520-555-0467.
cards.body: Same ten digits, yet the second version feels far easier to keep. Nothing about the numbers changed. What changed is how many things your mind has to juggle at once.

cards.headline: Working memory: the mind's workbench
cards.body: Short-term memory is best seen as one part of working memory: the few thoughts you're actively holding and using right now. You lean on it when you carry a digit in mental arithmetic, keep the start of a sentence in mind until it ends, or plan the order of your errands. It's where thinking happens, and the bench is surprisingly small.

cards.headline: Seven, then four
cards.body: In 1956, George Miller reviewed the research on short-term memory and found people can hold between 5 and 9 items. He called it "the magical number seven, plus or minus two." Later research revised it downward. When people can't rehearse or group items, young adults hold only about 3 to 5 chunks, and researchers led by Nelson Cowan now put working memory's capacity at about 4.

cards.headline: Chunking: packing more into each slot
cards.body: The limit counts chunks, not raw items. A chunk is any group your mind treats as one unit, so 520-555-0467 is three chunks, not ten digits. In Cowan's studies, word pairs people had learned together, like desk-ball, took up one slot, the same as a single word. Need bread, milk and pepper? Picture bread floating in peppery milk, and three items become one.

Afterward he forgot daily events almost as fast as they happened, yet he kept most of his older memories from before the operation. summary: Cues work best when they match how a memory was encoded, and a 1975 study found divers recalled words best where they learned them. A 2021 retest found no such advantage.

cards.headline: Divers learned words on land and underwater. Did the place matter?
cards.body: A 1975 study said yes, and it became one of the most retold experiments about memory. Decades later, someone put the divers back in the water to check.

cards.headline: Your memory files the setting too
cards.body: You don't store information in a vacuum; you encode it in a specific way, along with details of the moment. The encoding specificity principle says a cue works to the extent that it matches how the memory was stored. That's why an old song on the radio can bring back the whole party where you first heard it. The place where you learned something can act as a cue too.

cards.headline: The divers study
cards.body: In 1975, Godden and Baddeley had divers learn lists of spoken words either on land or underwater, then recall them in the same place or the other one. Recall was much better when the places matched: words learned underwater came back best underwater, and words learned on land came back best on land. Virtually every memory textbook came to describe it.

mascot.line: This is the lesson, not a footnote: a famous finding is only as strong as its retests. That's Level 1's publish-and-repeat idea at work.

cards.headline: The retest
cards.body: In 2021, Jaap Murre repeated the study with 16 divers in a heated indoor pool and found no advantage for recalling in the same place. The original used cold open water off Scotland, so the setups differ, and Murre concluded more replications are needed. The broader effect of context on recall is well established, but often weak. The divers result may simply be less solid than its fame.

title: The Forgetting Curve
objective: After this level you can explain how Hermann Ebbinghaus measured forgetting on himself and what shape the curve takes.
summary: Ebbinghaus tested himself with nonsense syllables and measured forgetting by how much faster he relearned lists. Forgetting is steep, then levels out; a 2015 retest matched it.

cards.headline: To study forgetting, one man spent seven months memorizing nonsense.
cards.body: Hermann Ebbinghaus was his own and only test subject, often running up to three sessions a day. In 1885 he published the results, including the famous forgetting curve.

cards.headline: Why nonsense?
cards.body: Ebbinghaus first tried learning stanzas of Byron's poem Don Juan, but their meanings varied too much to measure fairly. So he used nonsense syllables, short meaningless combinations like dax, bap and rif. Every item was about equally unfamiliar, which made one list a fair comparison with the next. He gave up realism to gain a clean measurement.

cards.headline: Measuring what's left: savings
cards.body: He learned each row of syllables until he could recite it twice without error, then relearned it after a delay of anywhere from 20 minutes to 31 days. The effort saved on relearning showed what memory survived. If a row first took 25 repetitions and later took 20, he had saved 20 percent. Savings can reveal a trace even when plain recall shows nothing, because relearning still goes faster.

cards.headline: The shape of forgetting
cards.body: His curve shows memory for new material dropping quickly at first and then leveling out, so most forgetting happens soon after learning. In 2015, Jaap Murre's team at the University of Amsterdam repeated the experiment, with one volunteer spending 70 hours learning and relearning lists. The results were similar to Ebbinghaus's. This classic passed its retest.

title: Study Tricks That Work
objective: After this level you can explain the spacing and testing effects and why rereading works less well than it feels.
summary: Practice testing and spaced study beat rereading and cramming. Retrieving a memory strengthens it, even though restudying feels more reassuring.

cards.headline: Rereading your notes feels like studying. Research says it barely helps.
cards.body: Most students reread and highlight, yet these habits don't consistently boost performance. Two other techniques do, and the evidence for them is strong.

cards.headline: Testing beats restudying
cards.body: In a 2006 study by Roediger and Karpicke, students read prose passages, then either took recall tests or restudied the same material. Five minutes later, the restudiers did better. But two days or a week later, the tested students remembered substantially more, even though restudying made students more confident. The act of pulling a memory out makes it easier to pull out again: the testing effect.

cards.headline: Spacing beats cramming
cards.body: Distributed practice means studying in several short sessions spread over time instead of one long cram. Memory consolidation takes time, and spacing gives memories that time. Ebbinghaus ran the first study of this spacing effect, and it is arguably the most replicable finding in experimental psychology.

mascot.line: Every question you answer here is practice testing. Now you know why the questions come after the cards.

cards.headline: The 2013 verdict
cards.body: A 2013 review led by John Dunlosky rated ten popular study techniques. Only two earned the top rating of high utility: practice testing and distributed practice. They helped learners of different ages and abilities on many kinds of tasks. Rereading and highlighting were rated low, and the advice was blunt: use practice testing instead of rereading.

title: Memory Rebuilds the Past
objective: After this level you can explain why remembering is reconstruction, using Frederic Bartlett's "War of the Ghosts" study.
summary: Bartlett (1932) had people retell a strange folktale over time. Their versions shrank and bent toward the familiar: remembering is reconstruction guided by schemas.

cards.headline: People retold a strange ghost story again and again. It kept changing.
cards.body: In 1932, the psychologist Frederic Bartlett reported that the changes followed a pattern. That pattern shows what remembering really is.

cards.headline: The War of the Ghosts
cards.body: Bartlett's participants, probably English college students, heard a Native American folktale called The War of the Ghosts. It is disjointed, full of supernatural events and rather hard to follow. They recalled it after 15 minutes, then again weeks, months or even years later. Each time, the story got shorter, and it didn't just lose pieces. It changed.

cards.headline: Making the strange familiar
cards.body: The changes weren't random. People rationalized the bizarre parts, reshaping the story to fit their own expectations and sometimes adding details to explain its oddities. Canoes became boats. These errors grew with each retelling. Bartlett traced them to schemas: general organizing structures of knowledge that guide how we take in and recall information.

cards.headline: Remembering is rebuilding
cards.body: Bartlett argued that understanding an event is a construction, so recalling it later means reconstructing it, not replaying a copy. Schemas help fill the gaps, and they also mislead: you might recall a beach umbrella in a beach scene that had none. Earlier retests of Bartlett had failed, but in 1999 Erik Bergman and Henry Roediger replicated it. After six months, most of what people recalled was distorted in some way.

title: Memories That Never Happened
objective: After this level you can explain how Elizabeth Loftus showed that leading questions and suggestion can create false memories.
summary: Elizabeth Loftus showed that information after an event can change memory of it: one word in a question altered speed estimates and planted broken glass. Whole false events can be implanted too.

cards.headline: Change one word in a question, and people remember glass that wasn't there.
cards.body: Elizabeth Loftus showed how easily memories can be edited after the fact. Her most famous experiment started with car crashes on film.

cards.headline: Smashed or contacted?
cards.body: In 1974, Loftus and John Palmer showed students films of car accidents and asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed," "collided," "bumped," "hit" or "contacted" each other. "Smashed" drew higher speed estimates than "contacted." A week later, people who had heard "smashed" were more than twice as likely to say they had seen broken glass. The film showed none.

cards.headline: The misinformation effect
cards.body: Misleading information you meet after an event can contaminate your memory of the event itself. Hundreds of studies have shown it, for everything from a small detail of a face to a barn that wasn't there. Even tiny wording matters: in a 1975 study, people were more likely to say yes to "Did you see the broken headlight?" than to "Did you see a broken headlight?"

cards.headline: Lost in the mall
cards.body: Could a whole event be planted? In a 1995 study by Loftus and Pickrell, students were asked about four childhood events supposedly supplied by relatives. One, getting lost in a shopping mall, was invented. After repeated questioning, a quarter came to believe it had happened. A preregistered 2023 replication with 123 people found 35 percent. Once planted, false memories are extremely hard to tell from true ones.

title: When Eyewitnesses Get It Wrong
objective: After this level you can explain why confident eyewitnesses can pick the wrong person and how lineups are made fairer.
summary: Eyewitness certainty can grow after confirming feedback, so a confident witness can be wrong. Double-blind, fair lineups with confidence recorded at once help.

cards.headline: A witness can be completely certain and completely wrong.
cards.body: In 1984 in North Carolina, a witness identified Ronald Cotton, and her testimony helped convict him. After more than 10 years in prison, he was cleared by DNA evidence. How does honest certainty go so wrong?

cards.headline: From "I think" to certain
cards.body: At the photo lineup, the witness first said, "I think this is the guy." The detective told her she did great. By the trial, she had absolutely no doubt. Psychologist Gary Wells points to exactly this kind of suggestive procedure, such as confirming a witness's choice, as what turns hesitation into certainty.

cards.headline: "Good, you identified the suspect"
cards.body: In a 1998 study by Gary Wells and Amy Bradfield, people watched a store security video and picked someone from a lineup that didn't contain the culprit. Those told "Good, you identified the suspect" later reported being more certain. A 2014 meta-analysis of about 7,000 participants found confirming feedback reliably inflates what witnesses report about their certainty, their view and their attention.

mascot.line: Keep this: the confidence that counts is the witness's first one, recorded at once, not the certainty they reach by the trial.

cards.headline: Fairer lineups
cards.body: In a double-blind lineup, the person running it doesn't know which member is the suspect, so they can't give cues. In a fair lineup, everyone matches the witness's description, so no one sticks out. The witness's confidence is recorded right away, before any feedback. Under clean conditions like these, a first, high-confidence pick is remarkably accurate, while a hesitant first pick is error prone.

title: Checkpoint: Memory

summary: Memory has three jobs: encoding, storage and retrieval. The chapter's studies each caught one going wrong, from the penny nobody encoded to memories rebuilt with details that never happened.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 finale: every memory slip is a failure at one of three steps.
cards.body: Memory is a set of processes that encode, store and retrieve information: getting it in, keeping it, and getting it back out. Each study in this chapter caught one of those jobs going wrong.

cards.headline: Encoding: you can't lose what you never stored
cards.body: Could you pick out a real US penny from a set of similar drawings? In a 1979 study by Raymond Nickerson and Marilyn Adams, most Americans couldn't, despite a lifetime of handling pennies. They had encoded only enough detail to tell a penny from other coins. Distraction while studying does the same thing: information that never gets encoded can't be remembered later.

title: What Gets You Moving
objective: After this level you can explain drives, homeostasis and incentives as sources of motivation.
summary: Motivation is what steers behavior toward a goal. Drives push from inside when the body slips out of balance, and incentives pull from the world outside.

cards.headline: Nobody pays you to drink when you're thirsty. Yet a paycheck works too.
cards.body: So what actually gets you moving? Psychologists define motivation as the wants or needs that direct behavior toward a goal. Their answers split in two: one force pushes from inside your body, and another pulls from out in the world.

cards.headline: Your body keeps a balance
cards.body: The first answer starts inside you. Your body works to hold things at a steady level, a balance called homeostasis. When it slips, say your blood sugar drops, you get a drive, hunger, that pushes you to eat until balance returns. Drive theory adds a twist: whatever ended the drive last time, you're likelier to do again. A snack that worked at 4 p.m. yesterday has a head start today.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: drives push from inside your body; incentives pull from outside. Most of what you do has a bit of both.

cards.headline: Pulled, not pushed
cards.body: Drives can't explain everything. Incentive theory says rewards and goals out in the world pull you toward them, while drives push from within, and most behavior mixes both. Even a lab animal shows the difference. In a Skinner box, an animal normally presses a bar for water when it's short of water. Under special conditions, it presses for water it doesn't need. No drive is pushing; the reward alone is pulling.

title: Maslow's Pyramid
objective: After this level you can explain Maslow's hierarchy of needs and what later research changed about it.
summary: Maslow's 1943 hierarchy ranks needs from food to self-actualization. He never drew the pyramid, said the order isn't rigid, and a 123-country study backs that up.

cards.headline: It's in almost every textbook. Maslow never drew it.
cards.body: Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs usually appears as a pyramid, with food at the bottom and fulfillment at the top. The needs are his. The pyramid, and the strict one-floor-at-a-time climb it suggests, came from someone else.

cards.headline: Five kinds of need
cards.body: In a 1943 paper, Maslow proposed a ladder of needs: physiological needs like food, then safety, love and belonging, esteem, and at the top self-actualization, which he called the desire to become everything one is capable of becoming. Lower needs generally come first. If you're struggling to find enough to eat, you're unlikely to worry much about how others see you.

cards.headline: Who built the pyramid?
cards.body: In 2019, Todd Bridgman and colleagues went looking for Maslow's pyramid and found he never drew one. They traced it to a 1960 article by Charles McDermid, a consulting psychologist. Maslow himself had warned, in that same 1943 paper, that his order was "not nearly as rigid" as it might sound; most people have every need only partly met at once.

cards.headline: What the world data say
cards.body: Then the idea met real numbers. In 2011, Louis Tay and Ed Diener looked at 123 countries. Meeting each need was linked to wellbeing largely regardless of whether other needs were met. Social needs mattered even where safety needs were unmet. The ladder turns out to be more of a web.

title: When Rewards Backfire
objective: After this level you can explain intrinsic and extrinsic motivation and how rewards can undermine interest.
summary: Doing something for its own sake is intrinsic motivation. An expected, tangible reward can shrink it, as preschoolers with magic markers showed in 1973.

cards.headline: Reward a child for drawing, and they may draw less.
cards.body: In 1973, at Stanford's Bing Nursery School, psychologists offered preschoolers who already loved drawing with magic markers a shiny Good Player Award. Weeks later, the children promised the award had cooled on drawing. How can a prize make a favorite activity less fun?

cards.headline: Two kinds of reason
cards.body: Psychologists split motivation into two kinds. Intrinsic motivation means you do something for the satisfaction it brings, like doodling because doodling is fun. Extrinsic motivation means you do it to get something from others: a grade, a paycheck, a gold star. Most of what you do mixes both. The trouble starts when one kind crowds out the other.

cards.headline: The Good Player Award
cards.body: Mark Lepper, David Greene and Richard Nisbett split the young artists into groups. Some were promised the award for drawing; some got it as a surprise afterward; some got nothing. One to two weeks later, observers watched free play. Children who had drawn for the expected award spent about 8.6 percent of their free time drawing, about half as much as the other two groups.

cards.headline: When rewards backfire
cards.body: This is the overjustification effect: an outside reward can shrink the inside reason, until effort depends on the reward. It isn't a one-off. A 1999 meta-analysis of 128 studies found expected and tangible rewards undermined intrinsic motivation, while positive feedback boosted it. Money tends to hurt more than praise, and a surprise reward tends to leave interest intact.

title: Willpower as a Battery?
objective: After this level you can explain the ego depletion theory and why large replication attempts failed to confirm it.
summary: Ego depletion claimed self-control is a limited resource that runs down. Large multi-lab replications in 2016 and 2021 found an effect near zero.

cards.headline: Can one plate of radishes drain your willpower?
cards.body: In 1998, Roy Baumeister and colleagues seated hungry people in a room that smelled of freshly baked cookies, and told some of them to eat radishes instead. The idea: willpower works like a battery that runs down. What happened next made the idea famous, and then it was tested again.

cards.headline: Radishes versus cookies
cards.body: The volunteers had skipped a meal. Chocolate chip cookies had been baked right in the room, next to chocolates and a bowl of radishes. The radish group had to resist; a few picked up cookies to sniff them, but no one bit. Next came puzzles that couldn't be solved. Radish eaters kept trying for about 8 minutes. Chocolate eaters lasted about 19, and a no-food group about 21.

cards.headline: A battery that runs down
cards.body: Baumeister's team concluded that self-control draws on a limited inner resource, and using it up leaves less for the next task. They called this ego depletion. The idea spread fast, and an early meta-analysis of the experiments found a medium-sized effect. Later meta-analyses questioned whether it was that big, or real at all, and found signs of possible bias.

mascot.line: Keep this: one striking study is a start. A result that holds up across many labs is what earns trust.

cards.headline: Twenty-three labs, then thirty-six
cards.body: So researchers tested it at scale. In 2016, a project led by Martin Hagger ran one standardized test in 23 labs with 2,141 people. The effect was near zero. In 2021, a test led by Kathleen Vohs in 36 labs with 3,531 people found no evidence for ego depletion in its planned analyses. The battery story made sense. The batteries just didn't show up.

title: What an Emotion Is
objective: After this level you can compare the James-Lange, Cannon-Bard and two-factor theories of emotion.
summary: James-Lange says arousal comes first, Cannon-Bard says arousal and feeling arrive together, and the two-factor theory says arousal plus a label makes an emotion.

cards.headline: A snake in the garden: does fear come first, or your pounding heart?
cards.body: You spot a venomous snake. Your heart races and fear floods in. It feels like one event, but psychologists have proposed different orders. Three theories give three answers, and one sneaky experiment put a label on the question.

cards.headline: Body first
cards.body: The James-Lange theory says emotions arise from bodily arousal. You see the snake, your heart races, and only then do you feel fear. The feeling is your reading of the body's alarm. It also held that different patterns of arousal produce different feelings, so fear and joy would each have their own bodily signature.

cards.headline: Both at once
cards.body: Critics doubted that the body's alarm differs enough between emotions to explain them all. If it looks much the same each time, it can't be what tells them apart. So the Cannon-Bard theory proposed that arousal and the feeling of emotion happen at the same time, but independently. Seeing the snake sets off the pounding heart and the fear together, on separate tracks.

cards.headline: Arousal plus a label
cards.body: The two-factor theory says an emotion is arousal plus a label you read from the situation. In 1962, Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer injected men with epinephrine, which mimics fight-or-flight. Only some were told what to expect; others heard of no effects or unrelated ones. Each then waited with an actor acting euphoric or angry. Men told what to expect felt no change. The others were likelier to report euphoria or anger that matched the actor.

title: Are Facial Expressions Universal?
objective: After this level you can explain Paul Ekman's evidence for universal expressions and the current debate over it.
summary: Ekman's 1971 study with the Fore suggested some facial expressions are universal. Lisa Feldman Barrett argues they vary far more than that, and the debate continues.

cards.headline: A photo of a face, shown to people with little outside contact.
cards.body: In 1971, Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen took photographs of faces to the Fore people of Papua New Guinea and asked a simple question: which face goes with this story? If people everywhere pick the same face, are expressions built in?

cards.headline: Ekman's case for universals
cards.body: Ekman and Friesen told short emotional stories and asked the Fore to choose the matching photographed face. Tasks like this, in small societies with little outside contact, gave strong evidence that people everywhere recognize the same expressions. Ekman's side adds that congenitally blind people, who never saw a face, move their faces much as sighted people do. Ekman's side lists seven: happiness, surprise, sadness, fear, disgust, contempt and anger.

cards.headline: Barrett's challenge
cards.body: In 2019, Lisa Feldman Barrett led a review that pushed back. Yes, people smile when happy and scowl when angry more often than chance. But how people express emotions varies a lot across cultures, situations and people. Most studies had people pick from a short list, which makes contrary evidence hard to find. Asked to name faces freely, people in small societies rarely gave the expected words. Trobriand Islanders read the wide-eyed gasp that Western studies call fear as a threat.

cards.headline: A debate still open
cards.body: Barrett proposes that emotions are constructed from experience, so one bodily state can become different emotions in different situations. The other side keeps finding support too: in 2021, Jessica Tracy's team reported that the Mayangna of Nicaragua recognized bodily expressions of anger, sadness and fear above chance. Both sides agree faces carry a lot of information. The argument is over how fixed and universal it is.

title: Does Smiling Make You Happier?
objective: After this level you can explain the facial feedback idea and why its replication record is mixed.
summary: The facial feedback idea says your expression can shape your feelings. The 1988 pen study failed a 17-lab replication, but deliberately posed smiles show a small effect.

cards.headline: Hold a pen between your teeth. Are cartoons funnier now?
cards.body: That was the claim of one of psychology's best-loved experiments. It rests on the facial feedback idea: that your face can affect the emotion you feel, not just show it. The pen test went into textbooks. Then many labs tried it again.

cards.headline: The pen study
cards.body: The facial feedback hypothesis says your expression can shape your emotion. In 1988, Fritz Strack and colleagues found a clever test. People held a pen in their mouth in ways that either engaged the smiling muscles or blocked them, without ever being asked to smile. Those in the smile position rated cartoons as funnier. No acting required, apparently.

cards.headline: Seventeen labs, almost nothing
cards.body: In 2016, 17 labs led by Eric-Jan Wagenmakers repeated the pen study, all following one shared protocol. In the original, the smile position made cartoons about 0.82 points funnier on a 10-point scale. Across the replications, the difference was 0.03. For the pen version, the effect all but vanished.

mascot.line: Keep the nuance: the pen study failed, but posed smiles still nudged happiness a little. Mixed is not the same as dead.

cards.headline: Many Smiles: a small nudge
cards.body: That wasn't the end. A 2019 meta-analysis led by Nicholas Coles found facial feedback has a small but highly variable effect. In 2022, the Many Smiles Collaboration, including researchers who disagreed, tested 3,878 people in 19 countries. Copying smiling faces or deliberately posing a smile raised happiness. The pen method was less conclusive.
