title: What Counts as a Mental Disorder
objective: After this level you can explain how clinicians distinguish a mental disorder from ordinary struggles and what the DSM is.
summary: A mental disorder is a significant disturbance in thinking, emotion or behavior, usually with distress or trouble functioning. The DSM classifies disorders, and its line moves with evidence.

cards.headline: Nearly 1 in 7 people worldwide live with a mental disorder.
cards.body: That was the World Health Organization's estimate for 2023: about 1.2 billion people. Yet everyone has bad days, nerves and grief. So where does an ordinary struggle end and a disorder begin?

mascot.line: Keep this: a disorder means real distress or trouble functioning, not just being different.

cards.headline: Unusual isn't enough
cards.body: The World Health Organization describes a mental disorder as a clinically significant disturbance in a person's thinking, emotion regulation or behavior. The American Psychiatric Association adds what usually comes with it: distress, or problems functioning at work, with family or with friends. Being unusual doesn't count on its own; red hair is uncommon, and it isn't a disorder. Neither does an expected reaction. Deep sadness after a loved one dies is grief, not a disorder by itself.

cards.headline: The manual on the shelf
cards.body: Clinicians work from a shared rulebook. In the United States it's the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, or DSM, published by the American Psychiatric Association. The first edition appeared in 1952; the current one, DSM-5-TR, in 2022. Its criteria spell out which symptoms must be present, and for how long. Psychiatrists, psychologists and counselors all use it. Much of the world relies on the World Health Organization's International Classification of Diseases, the ICD, for diagnosis.

cards.headline: When evidence moved the line
cards.body: The first DSM, in 1952, listed homosexuality as a disorder. In the late 1950s the psychologist Evelyn Hooker compared gay and straight men who weren't psychiatric patients, and found no more signs of psychological disturbance in the gay men. In 1973 the American Psychiatric Association concluded that disorders regularly bring distress or impairment, that homosexuality itself doesn't, and voted to remove it. The manual is a tool, and tools get corrected.

title: When Worry Won't Switch Off

summary: Anxiety is normal and often useful. In an anxiety disorder it doesn't go away and gets in the way of life; panic disorder and specific phobias are two examples.

cards.headline: Your heart pounds before a big exam. That's anxiety doing its job.
cards.body: Feeling anxious is a normal part of life, and it's useful: it pushes you to act and head off problems. So when does the same alarm become a disorder?

cards.headline: An alarm that won't reset
cards.body: In an anxiety disorder, the anxiety doesn't go away. It shows up in many situations, can get worse over time, and gets in the way of job performance, schoolwork and relationships. Anxiety and depressive disorders are the most common mental disorders worldwide. The practical line is simple: if anxiety starts causing problems in everyday life, at school, at work or with friends and family, NIMH advises talking to a health care provider.

title: Understanding Depression
objective: After this level you can explain how depression differs from sadness and why no single cause, such as a chemical imbalance, explains it.
summary: Depression is more than sadness. Genes, biology, environment and stress combine; the 'chemical imbalance' story is too simple, though antidepressants help many people.

cards.headline: Sadness is a feeling. Depression is a condition.
cards.body: Everyone feels low sometimes, and it usually passes. For years a tidy explanation for depression went around: a chemical imbalance. The research tells a bigger story.

cards.headline: More than a bad week
cards.body: Depression, also called major depressive disorder, is different from sadness. Its symptoms are severe enough to change how a person feels, thinks and manages sleep, eating or work. To be diagnosed, symptoms must be present most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks. A gloomy weekend is something else.

cards.headline: Not one chemical
cards.body: It's often said that depression is a chemical imbalance, but that phrase doesn't capture how complex it is. Research points to several factors acting together: genetic, biological, environmental and psychological, such as stressful life events. In 2022 a review led by Joanna Moncrieff found no consistent evidence that low serotonin causes depression. Other researchers disputed its methods, and pointed out that the serotonin theory never meant one chemical explains everything.

cards.fact: Twin studies put the heritability of major depression at about 37 percent.
cards.context: That estimate comes from a 2000 review by Patrick Sullivan and colleagues. Remember Level 7: heritability describes differences within a population, not any one person's fate. Genes matter here, and most of the variation still comes from elsewhere.

cards.headline: Too simple isn't useless
cards.body: Dropping the one-chemical story doesn't mean treatment fails. A 2018 analysis led by Andrea Cipriani pooled 522 trials and found that all 21 antidepressants it studied worked better than placebo for adults with depression. Decisions about medication, with or without talk therapy, are made by the person together with their doctor.

title: Beyond Anxiety and Depression
objective: After this level you can explain in general terms what ADHD, OCD, PTSD and bipolar disorder are, and why casual labels mislead.
summary: OCD, ADHD, bipolar disorder and PTSD are real conditions with specific features. Borrowing their names for everyday quirks blurs what they involve.

cards.headline: "I'm so OCD about my desk." Is that what OCD is?
cards.body: You've probably heard condition names used as casual labels. What people with OCD actually describe shows why that label misleads.

cards.headline: OCD isn't a love of tidiness
cards.body: In OCD, obsessions are intrusive, unwanted thoughts, urges or images that make most people anxious. Compulsions are repetitive behaviors a person feels driven to do, often in response. People with OCD don't enjoy their compulsions; they get only temporary relief from anxiety. They may spend more than an hour a day on them and can't stop, even knowing it's excessive. A tidy desk you enjoy is a preference. OCD is a loop that costs hours and brings no joy.

title: How Talk Therapy Works
objective: After this level you can explain what cognitive behavioral therapy does and what research says about how well therapy works.
summary: CBT, rooted in Aaron Beck's cognitive therapy, helps people question unhelpful thoughts and change what they do. A 1977 analysis of 375 studies found therapy helps on average.

cards.headline: Two people talk in a room once a week. Can that change how one feels?
cards.body: Stories of therapy helping are everywhere, but stories aren't evidence. In 1977 two researchers pulled together 375 studies to find out.

cards.headline: The psychiatrist who switched methods
cards.body: Aaron Beck, a psychiatrist, spent his early career studying psychoanalysis, Freud's talking cure from Level 4. He came to believe it lacked scientific rigor and evidence that it worked. So in the early 1960s he developed cognitive therapy, helping patients catch their "automatic" negative thoughts, the quick, gloomy verdicts that feed depression.

cards.headline: Thoughts, feelings, actions: one loop
cards.body: Cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT, grew from that work. A therapist helps a person change how they think and act, treating thoughts, feelings, body sensations and actions as linked. Together they question unhelpful thoughts and try other ways of seeing things. CBT focuses on current problems rather than the past, and most people have between 5 and 15 sessions. It's used for depression, anxiety, OCD and PTSD.

cards.fact: The average person in therapy ended up better off than 75 percent of untreated people.
cards.context: Mary Lee Smith and Gene Glass reached that in 1977 by combining 375 controlled studies. They found few important differences between quite different types of therapy. It's an average, not a promise: CBT may not work for everyone, and other treatments exist.

cards.body: Public stigma is the negative attitudes other people hold. Self-stigma is when a person turns those attitudes inward, as shame about their own condition. Structural stigma lives in policies that limit opportunities. Together they make people reluctant to seek help, or to stay with treatment once they start.

title: The Replication Crisis
objective: After this level you can explain why many psychology findings failed to replicate and what psychologists changed as a result.
summary: When 100 psychology studies were repeated in 2015, only about a third found their result again. Flexible analysis and publication bias explain much of it, and Registered Reports are one fix.

cards.headline: What happens when you rerun 100 published psychology studies?
cards.body: Level 1 said psychologists publish results so others can repeat them. In 2015 a large team, the Open Science Collaboration, actually did that for 100 studies at once. The results shook the field.

mascot.line: Keep this: one striking result is a lead, not a law. Repeats decide.

cards.fact: Only 36 percent of the repeated studies found a significant result again.
cards.context: Of the 100 originals, from three psychology journals, 97 percent had reported significant results. On the repeats, effects averaged about half their original size. That gap became the headline of what's called the replication crisis.

cards.headline: How to make the Beatles take years off
cards.body: In 2011 Joseph Simmons, Leif Nelson and Uri Simonsohn showed how false findings get made. Using flexible choices that are easy to leave unreported, like when to stop collecting data or which measures to report, they "found" that listening to the Beatles song "When I'm Sixty-Four" made people nearly a year and a half younger. Impossible, of course. That was the point: undisclosed flexibility can make almost anything look significant.

cards.headline: Fixing the pipeline
cards.body: Psychologists changed how studies get published. In a Registered Report, a journal peer-reviews the plan before any data are collected and accepts it in principle, whatever the results. That removes the reward for tiny samples, selective reporting and publication bias, the tilt toward positive results. The format began around 2013 at the journal Cortex, and over 300 journals now offer it.

options.label: Journals accept the plan before the results are known
Only studies with positive results get published

options.rationale: Registered Reports are still published openly.

title: Power Posing: Rise and Fall
objective: After this level you can trace how the power posing finding spread and weigh what replications later showed.
summary: A 2010 study said 'power poses' changed hormones and behavior, and a TED talk made it famous. Larger replications failed; only a small, debated effect on felt power remains.

cards.headline: Stand like a superhero for two minutes and change your hormones?
cards.body: That was the promise of power posing. It spread around the world. Then other researchers checked.

cards.headline: The rise
cards.body: In 2010 Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap had 42 people hold either expansive "high-power" poses or closed "low-power" ones, for one minute each. They reported that high-power poses raised feelings of power, testosterone and risk taking, and lowered the stress hormone cortisol. In 2012 Cuddy's TED talk on the idea became one of the most watched TED talks ever.

cards.headline: The fall
cards.body: In 2015 Eva Ranehill and colleagues tested power posing with 200 people. They found no effect on hormones or on risk taking, though people did report feeling more powerful. In 2016 the original lead author, Dana Carney, wrote: "I do not believe that 'power pose' effects are real." She called the original sample tiny and the data flimsy.

cards.headline: What's left, and why to be careful
cards.body: Later large analyses found one surviving effect: posture can shift how powerful people say they feel. The hormone and behavior effects are largely unsupported, and how much the felt-power effect means is still debated. Notice where it survived: a self-report. Carney also wrote that the original self-report measure was p-hacked: many power questions were asked, and the ones that "worked" were reported.

cards.headline: Power posing, weighed
learned: 2010: 42 people, one-minute poses, big claims
2015: 200 people, no hormone or behavior effects
2016: the lead author said the effect isn't real
Left: a small, debated effect on felt power

No effects of any kind, even on feelings

options.rationale: The hormone effects didn't replicate.

options.label: Proven to change both hormones and bold behavior
options.rationale: Larger studies found no hormone or behavior effects.

options.label: Fully disproven, even for how people feel inside
options.rationale: A small effect on felt power remains, though it's debated.

options.label: It works, but only when held for over an hour
options.rationale: No study here tested anything like that.

options.label: Small, debated felt-power effect; no hormone or behavior effect

questions.explanation: The hormone and behavior claims failed to replicate; a small, debated effect on self-reported power is what's left.

options.label: People can misremember or answer to look good
Self-reports can't be collected from large groups
options.rationale: Surveys collect them from many people easily.

options.label: Self-reports need hormone tests to count
options.rationale: They're a separate kind of measure.

questions.explanation: Self-reports are useful but fallible, and Carney said the original self-report measure was p-hacked.

title: Spotting Psychology Myths
objective: After this level you can weigh popular claims, like learning styles and venting anger, against the research evidence.
summary: Two popular claims, tested: matching teaching to 'learning styles' has virtually no evidence behind it, and venting anger tends to feed it rather than drain it.

cards.headline: "I'm a visual learner." "Let it out, you'll feel better."
cards.body: Both sound like common sense, and both come with a theory. Learning styles says teaching should match how you like to learn. Venting says anger drains away once you release it. Here's what happened when researchers tested them.

cards.headline: Learning styles: preference isn't proof
cards.body: The learning-styles idea says you learn best when teaching matches your preferred mode, like pictures for a "visual learner". It's widespread in education, from kindergarten to graduate school. And people do have preferences: ask, and almost anyone will name one. But liking a format and learning better from it are two different claims.

cards.headline: What the evidence showed
cards.body: In 2008 Harold Pashler and colleagues reviewed the research. They found plenty of evidence that people state preferences, but virtually no evidence that matching teaching to them improves learning. Some well-designed studies flatly contradicted it. Their advice: spend limited education budgets on practices with strong evidence instead.

mascot.line: It connects: this is Level 4's Freud again, and again the tested details didn't hold.

cards.headline: Venting feeds the flame
cards.body: The idea of venting goes back to Josef Breuer and Sigmund Freud, who held that expressing pent-up emotion beats bottling it up: anger as pressure that needs a release valve. In 2002 Brad Bushman tested it. Angered people who hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who angered them felt angrier and acted more aggressively than people who did nothing. Doing nothing beat venting.

cards.headline: Myths, tested
learned: People state learning preferences, but matching doesn't help
Spend on teaching methods with strong evidence
Venting anger tends to feed it
Popular claims get weighed by what the experiments found

questions.prompt: In Brad Bushman's 2002 study, how did people who hit a punching bag while thinking about their provoker end up?

options.label: Calmer than the people who did nothing at all

options.label: Angrier and more aggressive than the do-nothing group
Too tired to feel much anger at all
options.rationale: The study measured more anger and aggression.

questions.explanation: Venting while dwelling on the provoker increased anger and aggression; doing nothing worked better.

options.label: Students don't have any preferences at all
options.rationale: They do state preferences; matching them just doesn't help.

questions.explanation: Pashler's review found virtually no evidence that matching teaching to learning styles improves learning.

title: Mastery Challenge: Psychology
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Psychology Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: One question from each chapter, from the first psychology lab to the replication crisis: what we notice, learn, remember, feel and judge. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Psychology Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from across the tree, from the first psychology lab to the replication crisis. Level 1 asked how you study a mind nobody can see. Now show how far you've come. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Psychology: mastered
learned: How psychology tests ideas about an unseen mind, from Wundt's lab to the replication crisis.
How perception, learning and memory filter, shape and rebuild what you experience and do.
Why mental shortcuts, other people and the way you judge events steer what you feel and decide.
How minds change across a life, and how to talk about mental health without stigma.

questions.prompt: What made Wundt's 1879 Leipzig lab the start of psychology as a science?

options.label: He brought experiments to questions philosophy had only argued over
He was the first to treat patients with talk therapy
options.rationale: Talk therapy was Freud's psychoanalysis.

options.label: He showed the mind works like a computer
options.rationale: That picture came with the cognitive revolution, decades later.

options.label: He studied only behavior anyone could observe
options.rationale: That was Watson's behaviorism.

questions.explanation: Wundt set up the first psychology lab in 1879 and insisted on experiments borrowed from the natural sciences.

options.label: The McGurk effect

options.label: Weber's law
options.rationale: That's about the smallest change in a stimulus you can notice.

options.label: Inattentional blindness
Subliminal perception

questions.prompt: Sunglasses stop the glare that hurts your eyes, so you start reaching for them sooner. In Learning and Habits terms, what is this?

options.label: Positive punishment
options.rationale: Nothing unpleasant is added, and the behavior goes up, not down.

options.label: Negative reinforcement
Negative punishment
options.rationale: Punishment makes a behavior less likely; here it grows.

options.label: Classical conditioning
options.rationale: Your action brings a consequence, which is operant learning.

questions.explanation: Something unpleasant is taken away (negative) and the behavior increases (reinforcement), like the seatbelt beep that stops when you buckle up.

questions.prompt: Ana rereads her notes in one long session the night before a test. Ben quizzes himself in short sessions across the week. Who likely remembers more a week later?

options.label: Ana, because rereading builds the most confidence
options.rationale: Restudiers felt surer but remembered less days later.

options.label: Both the same, since total study time is what counts
options.rationale: How you study matters, not just how long.

options.label: Ana, because one long session keeps it fresh for weeks
options.rationale: Spaced sessions beat cramming for lasting memory.

options.label: Ben, because retrieving and spacing both strengthen memory

options.label: Social needs mattered to wellbeing even where safety was unmet
People met their needs strictly one floor at a time
options.rationale: Each need mattered largely regardless of the others.

options.label: Only food and safety were linked to wellbeing
options.rationale: Meeting each need was linked to wellbeing.

options.label: Maslow's own pyramid had predicted this exact order

options.rationale: That's about judging people, not risks.

Hindsight bias: outcomes seem obvious once you know them
options.rationale: That's about rewriting past predictions.

questions.prompt: A 3-year-old sees a friend leave, then watches Mom move the friend's toy from a box to a drawer. Asked where the friend will look, the child points to the drawer. What does that suggest?

options.label: The child has passed the false-belief test early

questions.prompt: A new coworker says little in her first meeting, and you decide she's just shy. You never weigh that it's her first day among strangers. What is this?

options.label: Festinger's cognitive dissonance
options.rationale: That's changing an attitude to fit your own actions.

Favoring your own in-group

The body's reaction alone fixes the emotion you feel

options.label: One striking result in a top journal
options.rationale: Many such results failed on a rerun.

options.label: A famous talk that millions have watched
options.rationale: Power posing had that, and still faded.

options.label: How confident the original author is
options.rationale: Confidence isn't evidence.

options.label: Other researchers repeat it and find it again
